summary:
Kuwait's National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Article 198 in 2007, criminalising an indecent act in a public place or imitating the appearance of a member of the opposite sex, with penalties of up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). Human Rights Watch found that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor obtain protection from the policing it authorised. The amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support.

Enforcement began immediately and violently. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, in coffee shops and in taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against transgender women pursued under the provision, and in 2017 a social-media personality known as King Luxy was detained for two weeks in Kuwait on suspicion of looking too feminine.

In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck the 2007 "imitating the opposite sex" provision down as unconstitutional, a ruling recorded by the Library of Congress and confirmed in HRW's World Report 2024. The challenge was brought by an individual targeted by police. HRW urged the National Assembly to repeal the provision outright, noting that the judgment removed criminal exposure but did not end the underlying dress-code policing practice; analysis by the Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute in July 2024 set out the steps still required after abolition.

Trans visitors remain exposed through other provisions. Penal Code Article 193 punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years, adultery by up to five, and public morality laws are strictly enforced with regular prosecutions. In February 2023 DAWN reported that a year after the ruling transgender discrimination continued in practice, with social and employment discrimination persisting and no movement toward recognition of transgender rights. Officials continue to act on the presumption that gender non-conformity is suspect, whatever the constitutional position.

Entry and screening carry separate risks. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council states agreed to discuss a proposal for some form of testing to detect homosexuality in order to deny entry to gay foreigners; officials later insisted it was only a proposal, with concern over hosting the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar cited as a reason for backtracking. Foreign nationals found to be infected with HIV are deported, while Kuwaiti citizens are entitled to outpatient care through a specialised infectious disease hospital. No association or charity exists in Kuwait to campaign for LGBTQ rights or to organise community events.

State censorship and official invisibility reinforce the risk. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material including advocacy and legal information, no candidate stood for the National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation, and in August 2023 Kuwait banned the film "Barbie" on the stated grounds that it promoted homosexuality. Censors had also banned "The Danish Girl" among other films, and gender segregation and enforced dress codes across the region make gender-non-conforming visitors especially visible to scrutiny.
tangentialFactors:
Kuwait's regime does not operate in isolation. Regional norms of gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans visitors unusually legible to casual policing, and cross-dressing is a crime across a number of Middle Eastern jurisdictions, a pattern Brian Whitaker surveyed in 2016.

HRW's 2018 regional study "Audacity in Adversity" drew on interviews with 34 activists across 22 jurisdictions including Kuwait, and found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or activism. The pattern of outward movement is a signal about the durability of local protection.

Kuwait's HIV prevalence has remained below 0.1 percent through the latest 2021 figures, with males aged 25 to 49 accounting for 47 percent of those living with HIV. The National Assembly criminalised intentional transmission of HIV in 1992. Deportation of infected foreign nationals is the practical consequence for a visitor, not care.
localsOnly:
Kuwaiti citizens remain subject to Penal Code Article 193, which punishes consensual same-sex relations between men by up to seven years and adultery by up to five, and the 1992 statute on intentional HIV transmission. Citizens diagnosed with HIV are entitled to outpatient medical care organised by a specialised infectious disease hospital, a provision that does not extend to foreign nationals.

Social and employment discrimination against transgender people persisted as of February 2023, according to DAWN's assessment a year after the Constitutional Court ruling, and the judgment was not treated as a first step toward recognising transgender rights. No mechanism for changing legal gender documents is documented in the sources.

Organised advocacy remains blocked. In 2007 a group of Kuwaitis applied to the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs to form an LGBTQ rights association and never received a formal reply; in July 2019 they announced they would reapply after a Ministry of Commerce crackdown on LGBTQ symbols such as rainbow displays in shops. Political participation stays invisible: no candidate has run for the National Assembly openly acknowledging LGBTQI+ orientation, and there is no known association or charity campaigning for LGBTQ rights or running educational and social events.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the National Assembly has since deleted Article 199 bis from the Penal Code text, as distinct from the Constitutional Court's annulment of its application, is unresolved in the available sources; HRW's call for outright repeal is recorded but no legislative outcome is.

The practical enforcement picture after February 2022 is not sourced beyond DAWN's February 2023 assessment and the general statement that discrimination by officials persists. Arrest, stop-and-search and documentation-check data for transgender visitors since the ruling is not available here.

The procedure, fee and evidentiary requirements for changing gender markers on Kuwaiti identity or travel documents are not documented in this inventory, so the current documentary position for a trans visitor is stated only as the absence of any recognised route.

The 2013 Gulf Cooperation Council entry-testing proposal is recorded as a proposal that officials later disowned; whether any element of it was implemented, by Kuwait or by any other state in the council, is unresolved. The stated ground for the August 2023 "Barbie" ban comes from the authorities' own announcement and is reproduced as such rather than independently verified.
